What is happening to people’s health?

We are examining verified hospital data on respiratory outpatient visits, emergency admissions and smog-related illnesses. Our records indicate a decline in respiratory patients, and the exact figures and reporting periods should be published alongside the findings.

title: Targeting Accelerated Aging in COPD: The AMICO (A Trial of Metformin In COpd) Trial Design.
text: INTRODUCTION: Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) is increasingly recognized as a disease of accelerated biological aging characterized by progressive lung function decline, emphysema progression and multiple age-related comorbidities. Current therapies improve symptoms and reduce exacerbations but have limited effects on disease progression. Metformin has demonstrated anti-aging properties through modulation of pathways involved in oxidative stress, inflammation, mitochondrial dysfunction and cellular senescence, making it a potential disease-modifying treatment in COPD. METHODS: AMICO (A Trial of Metformin In COPD) is an investigator-initiated, multicenter, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled phase III trial conducted in anonymous. A total of 212 patients with clinically stable COPD, centrilobular emphysema on computed tomography, post-bronchodilator FEV1 40%-70% predicted and accelerated FEV1 decline (>40 mL·year-1) will be randomized (1:1) to receive metformin (850 mg twice daily) or matching placebo for 36 months in addition to standard COPD treatment. Assessments include pulmonary function, chest computed tomography, exercise capacity, health status, muscle strength, body composition, age associated comorbidities development and aging-related biomarkers.The primary endpoint is the annual rate of FEV1 decline over 36 months. Secondary endpoints include emphysema progression, changes in diffusing capacity, COPD Assessment Test score, 6-minute walk distance, BODE index, handgrip strength, exacerbations, major cardiovascular events, cancer incidence and renal dysfunction. CONCLUSIONS: AMICO is the first randomized trial specifically designed to evaluate metformin as a gerotherapeutic and disease-modifying intervention in COPD. The study may provide novel evidence supporting geroscience-based approaches to slow disease progression and improve long-term outcomes in patients with COPD.

title: Mucus Plugging Across Multiple Chronic Respiratory Diseases: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis.
text: OBJECTIVE: To systematically evaluate the prevalence, clinical characteristics, and clinical outcomes of mucus plugging across chronic respiratory diseases. METHODS: Two authors searched four databases for eligible studies. Prevalence of mucus plugging was pooled and shown as percentage with a 95% confidence intervals (CI). Differences in clinical characteristics were summarized using mean differences or odds ratios, with corresponding 95% CIs. Sensitivity analyses, subgroup analyses and meta-regression were conducted for heterogeneity assessments. Associations between mucus plugging and clinical outcomes were systematically evaluated. RESULTS: A total of 33 studies was included. Prevalence of mucus plugging in asthma, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) and cystic fibrosis reached 63% (95%CI 52%, 74%), 47% (95% CI 38%, 55%) and 63% (95% CI 46%, 81%) respectively. Mucus plugging was associated with higher eosinophil counts and FeNO, and lower FEV₁% and FEV₁/FVC in asthma, as well as higher smoking odds. In COPD, mucus plugging was associated with older age and lower BMI, FEV₁%, FVC% and FEV₁/FVC (all p < 0.05). Meta-regression suggested that eosinophil counts (p < 0.01), FeNO (p = 0.02) and FEV1% (p=0.04) contributed to heterogeneity in asthma, and inhaled corticosteroid (p < 0.01) and FEV1/FVC (p < 0.01) contributed to heterogeneity in COPD. Presence of mucus plugging was also associated with higher risk of acute exacerbation, mortality, prolonged hospital stays and increased hospitalization costs in patients with COPD. CONCLUSION: Mucus plugging is prevalent in chronic respiratory diseases and associated with distinct clinical characteristics and outcomes. Future research may focus on mucus plugging as a treatable trait to improve prognosis of these patients.
author_name: Dongru Du, Suli Liu, Yin Zhang et al.

title: Meta-analysis of empirical evidence on biodiversity and the risk of asthma.
text: Climate change and urbanization are associated with reduced greenness and vegetation diversity, depletion of biodiversity, and impoverishment of human microbiota. These changes may influence immune regulation and increase the risk of many chronic inflammatory diseases, such as asthma. This study presents the results of a meta-analysis of the association between exposure to environmental and human microbiota biodiversity and the development of asthma. The effect estimates for biodiversity were summarized as the standardized mean difference or relative risk with 95% confidence interval applying the Hedges method and the restricted maximum likelihood estimator, respectively. The summary effect estimates for the association between environmental biodiversity, using the Shannon index, and asthma was not statistically significant; whereas higher bacterial richness showed a significant protective association with asthma, although the considerable heterogeneity across the studies and publication bias. For human microbiota diversity, the summary standardized mean difference suggested that the risk of asthma was associated with high bacterial diversity and bacterial richness/abundance, while the OR‑based estimate for bacterial richness and asthma was not significant. Our meta-analysis shows variable associations between exposure to environmental and human microbiota biodiversity and asthma, with the direction and magnitude of these associations depending on the specific biodiversity metrics and analytical approaches used.
